title: August and the Radiators
premise: Ansel Quintana, once a celebrated piano prodigy who vanished from the conservatory at twenty-two, returns a decade later as its night janitor, mopping floors beneath the practice rooms where her old life still echoes. When she hears a student performing 'August and the Radiators'—a song her late mentor wrote for her and never recorded—she realizes someone has been keeping his unfinished work alive, and that the song's final movement was left to her alone. As the conservatory faces closure and the student, a defiant girl named Wren, demands to know who Ansel really is, Ansel must choose between the safety of anonymity and the loyalty owed to the dead. In the end, she plays the completed song aloud at the building's last concert, claims both her name and her grief, and takes Wren on as her first student—a found family built not on blood but on music passed hand to hand.
about_author: Oscar Ravensworth is the pen name of a former conservatory custodian who spent eleven years listening to practice rooms through the walls before writing a word. Their fiction explores the quiet lives of people who almost became legends.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Third-person limited POV following Ansel through her nightly rounds: buffing the stage, avoiding the practice wing, memorizing schedules so she never meets anyone. She treats the conservatory like a rented room in someone else's life. Emotional beat: the numb safety of invisibility, and the first hairline crack in it when she pauses outside Room 7 without knowing why.

chapters.title: Room Seven
chapters.summary: Still Ansel's POV. A girl named Wren practices past midnight, playing something Ansel recognizes with her whole body: 'August and the Radiators,' written by her mentor Elias and performed only twice, never recorded. Ansel flees mid-phrase. Emotional beat: grief ambushing her in a mop closet; the past refusing to stay buried.

chapters.title: What Elias Left
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter in Ansel's POV, braided into one present-tense night shift. We learn of Elias's illness, his refusal to record the song until Ansel could play it 'without flinching,' and her flight from the conservatory before he died. Emotional beat: guilt revealed as the true architecture of her disappearance.

chapters.title: Wren
chapters.summary: POV shifts to Wren, a scholarship student who found the song in a donated folder of Elias's papers and taught herself its two movements. She's noticed the janitor who listens at doors. She leaves sheet music deliberately on a cart—an invitation or a trap. Emotional beat: loneliness recognizing loneliness across an impossible social gulf.

chapters.title: Closure Notice
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The conservatory announces it will close in spring; Wren's scholarship dies with it, and Ansel's job too. The dean plans a farewell gala. Wren wants to perform the unrecorded song there; the dean refuses anything 'unverifiable.' Emotional beat: shared stakes forcing two strangers toward each other.

chapters.title: The Third Movement
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. She admits to herself that Elias left the third movement unfinished on purpose—it exists only as fragments in her memory of their last lesson. She begins reconstructing it at night on the auditorium piano, hands remembering what pride forbade. Emotional beat: the terrifying tenderness of making again after years of only maintaining.

chapters.title: Caught Listening
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren discovers Ansel mid-rehearsal and confronts her; Ansel denies everything, then can't sustain the lie against a girl who plays Elias's phrasing like breathing. Partial confession: she knew Elias, nothing more. Wren doesn't believe her—and asks her to teach her the third movement anyway. Emotional beat: loyalty to a stranger's memory beginning to outweigh self-protection.

chapters.title: The Dean's Offer
chapters.summary: Ansel's POV. The dean, an old classmate who recognizes her hands, offers to restore her name and career if she performs at the gala—as a legend returned, the story sanitized. Accepting means letting the institution own Elias's song and erasing Wren's role in keeping it alive. Emotional beat: the seduction of redemption on someone else's terms.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: Climax, alternating POV. At the gala, the dean introduces the sanitized program; instead, Ansel walks out in her janitor's uniform, names herself and Elias and Wren from the stage, and premieres the completed 'August and the Radiators' with Wren at the second piano. The room learns the truth all at once. Emotional beat: grief spoken aloud finally becoming love instead of debt.

chapters.title: First Lesson
chapters.summary: Resolution, Wren's POV. Spring: the conservatory is sold, but Wren and Ansel share a rented studio above a hardware store where the radiators knock like applause. Ansel gives Wren Elias's folder and her first real lesson. Emotional beat: the song survives by being given away; family is whoever you keep practicing with.
